_note: Style-guide retrieval test set for the grammar and feedback tasks. Each case is a short draft with one known problem; gold snippets are guide passages that contain the actual rule or advice for it (not just a heading or a list entry). When a case has several snippets, ANY of them is useful advice on its own. The eval builds the query the way the task does (retrieval_query + draft) and also tests other query styles. Drafted by Claude.

cases.issue: weak intensifiers and qualifiers
cases.draft: The results of the survey were quite surprising and really very important for the company. It is extremely clear that customers are rather unhappy with the new design, and the team was totally convinced that a change was absolutely necessary.

gold.snippet: Delete weak intensifiers and qualifiers; sentences are more forceful without them

cases.issue: redundant words and phrases
cases.draft: In my personal opinion, the final outcome of the study was the end result of past history. The researchers joined together in close proximity and repeated again the experiment, which was completely finished by the month of May.

gold.snippet: any student could randomly sit delete "any" and "randomly"

cases.issue: contractions and informal register in an academic text
cases.draft: Climate policy isn't something governments can ignore anymore. They've tried to delay it, but that won't work forever :) Basically, it's a huge deal and everybody knows it, so we shouldn't wait any longer.

gold.file: data/styles/formal/Guidelines for Effective Professional and Academic .pdf
gold.snippet: contractions (such as "can't"), emoticons (smiley faces)

gold.file: data/styles/formal/Guidelines for Effective Professional and Academic .pdf
gold.snippet: Remember to take out contractions

cases.issue: first and second person in a formal essay
cases.draft: I think this policy is a mistake. You should know that I have read many reports, and in my view you can clearly see that the costs are too high. I feel that we need to reconsider the whole approach.

gold.file: data/styles/formal/Guidelines for Effective Professional and Academic .pdf
gold.snippet: avoid addressing the reader (i.e., using "you should know...") or using first person (i.e., "i think this is...")

cases.issue: no clear thesis: the introduction lists topics without a central claim
cases.draft: Social media is used by many people. There are many platforms such as Instagram and TikTok. Some people use it for news and others for entertainment. In this essay I will talk about social media and some of its aspects.

gold.snippet: Your thesis is the central claim in your essay-your main insight or idea about your source or topic. your thesis should appear early in an academic essay

cases.issue: paragraph without a topic sentence
cases.draft: In 2019, the city added two bus lines. Ticket prices fell by ten per cent. Some residents said they still preferred driving. Parking fees went up in the centre. A survey found that cycling had also increased slightly.

gold.snippet: strong topic sentence makes a claim or states a main idea that is then developed in the rest of the paragraph

cases.issue: missing transitions between ideas
cases.draft: Renewable energy has become cheaper. Many countries still depend on coal. Solar panels need a lot of space. Governments offer subsidies. Wind farms are often opposed by local residents. The climate targets for 2030 are ambitious.

gold.snippet: your goal should be to help readers see how your ideas are connected

cases.issue: vague email subject line
cases.draft:
Subject: Question

Dear Professor Miller,
I had a question about the assignment that is due next week and wanted to ask whether we can submit it a few days later because of the field trip.
Best regards,
Anna

gold.file: data/styles/formal/Effective Email Communication – The Writing Center.pdf
gold.snippet: they should convey the main point of your message or the idea that you want the reader to take away. therefore, be as specific as possible

cases.issue: literature review that only summarises sources one by one
cases.draft: Smith (2018) studied remote work and found that productivity increased. Jones (2020) also studied remote work and found that employees felt lonely. Brown (2021) looked at managers and found that they preferred office work. Lee (2022) studied remote work in Asia.

gold.snippet: A summary is a recap of the important information of the source, but a synthesis is a re-organization

cases.issue: book review that only retells the plot
cases.draft: The novel begins when Clara moves to London. She finds a job in a bakery and meets Tom. Then her mother falls ill and she goes back home. Later Tom visits her and they decide to open their own shop. At the end the shop is a success.

gold.snippet: the most important element of a review is that it is a commentary, not merely a summary

cases.issue: comma splice
cases.draft: The rain had stopped by the time Mara reached the harbour, the boats were already coming in. She waited by the wall, her coat was still dripping. Nobody looked at her, everyone was busy with the nets.

gold.snippet: When two complete sentences are joined by a comma, the result is a comma splice

cases.issue: fused (run-on) sentences
cases.draft: The door creaked open nobody was inside. Elias stepped into the hall the floorboards groaned under his boots. He called his brother's name there was no answer.

gold.snippet: When two complete sentences are combined into one without any punctuation, the result is a fused sentence

cases.issue: subject-verb agreement
cases.draft: The soldiers at the gate was tired after the long night. Each of the horses were restless, and the captain, together with his two sergeants, were arguing about the route. The list of supplies were shorter than expected.

gold.snippet: the subject of a sentence and the verb of a sentence must agree with each other in number

cases.issue: agreement with neither/nor and either/or
cases.draft: Neither the twins nor their father want to leave the village. Either the innkeeper or his daughters knows the way through the forest, but neither the map nor the stories agrees on where the path begins.

gold.snippet: The verb must agree with the subject that is nearest to the verb

cases.issue: passive voice and wordy 'to be' constructions
cases.draft: The letter was found by Ellen under the stairs. It was decided by her that it should be read later. The candle was lit and the window was closed, and it was felt by everyone in the house that something had been hidden from them.

gold.snippet: Sentences with passive-voice verbs often create confusion, because the subject of the sentence does not perform an action

cases.issue: point of view switches from first person to third person
cases.draft: I had never seen the lighthouse so dark. My hands shook as I climbed the stairs. Jonah reached the top and looked out at the sea. He wondered whether his sister had seen the ship before the storm took it. I pushed open the door.

gold.snippet: Do not begin your story with a first person narrator and then switch to a third person narrator
establish the point of view within the first two paragraphs of your story

cases.issue: third person limited suddenly becomes omniscient
cases.draft: Anna pushed open the café door and looked for an empty table. She was tired after the long shift and wanted only a coffee. The waiter, who had been secretly planning to quit for weeks, thought she looked familiar. In the corner, an old man remembered the war and wondered whether his son would ever call.

gold.snippet: do not start with third person limited point of view and then abruptly give your narrator full omniscience

cases.issue: telling emotions instead of showing them
cases.draft: Sarah was very sad. She was sad because her dog had died. Her father was angry, and her brother was also upset. The whole family felt terrible, and the house felt empty and sad for a long time.

gold.snippet: don't generalize a feeling with a summary sentence or two, put us in the immediacy of the moment, and rely on scenic detail
Showing is another way to talk about the inclusion of images in your writing. images are not only visual. they include all five senses

cases.issue: nested quotation marks in British style
cases.draft: "I heard her say "never again" before she left," said Tom. Later the vicar remarked, "The phrase "fraudulent conversion" will never stick."

gold.snippet: use double quotes within single quotes for a quotation within a quotation

cases.issue: dangling modifiers
cases.draft: Walking through the forest at dusk, the trees seemed to lean closer. Tired and hungry, the cabin finally appeared between the pines. After lighting the fire, the room grew warm and the storm outside was forgotten.

gold.snippet: A dangling modifier is a word, phrase, or clause that describes something that has been left out of the sentence
